nameStory: The mouse-eared snail gets its charming name from its tiny, rounded shell that resembles the delicate ear of a mouse. The scientific name Myosotella even comes from the Greek words for 'mouse ear,' making this one of those perfect cases where both the common and scientific names tell the same adorable story!
description: The mouse-eared snail is a tiny European snail that has made its home in New England's salt marshes. These miniature mollusks are terrestrial, meaning they live on land rather than underwater, but they stick close to salty, coastal environments. Their small, brownish shells are so petite you might walk right past dozens of them without noticing. Despite being called terrestrial, they're closely tied to the rhythm of the tides and saltwater influence.

idTips.label: Shell size and shape
idTips.description: Look for an incredibly small, oval shell that could easily fit on your pinky nail with room to spare - it truly does look like a tiny mouse ear when viewed from the side

idTips.label: Color pattern
idTips.description: The shell appears brownish or amber-colored, often with a slightly glossy sheen when wet from marsh moisture

idTips.label: Habitat preference
idTips.description: Always found in salt marsh areas where you can smell the briny ocean air and feel the spongy, salt-saturated soil underfoot

idTips.label: Shell texture
idTips.description: The shell feels smooth to the touch when you can find one large enough to handle, lacking the ridges or spirals of many other small snails

idTips.label: Location on plants
idTips.description: Often spotted climbing on salt marsh grasses and other halophytic plants that can tolerate salty conditions

habitat: Mouse-eared snails live exclusively in New England's salt marshes, particularly in areas with cordgrass, glasswort, and other salt-tolerant vegetation. You'll find them in the upper reaches of tidal marshes where saltwater influence is strong but not constantly submerged. Look for them along the Maine, New Hampshire, and Massachusetts coasts where protected bays and estuaries create ideal salt marsh conditions.

seasonality.spring: Active snails begin emerging as temperatures warm, often visible climbing on new growth of salt marsh plants during lower tides.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when snails are most visible and active, often found grazing on salt-tolerant plants during morning hours before heat peaks.
seasonality.fall: Snails remain active but may be harder to spot as they prepare for winter, often found closer to the base of vegetation.
seasonality.winter: Largely inactive and hidden, though empty shells may be easier to spot against dormant brown marsh grasses after storm tides.

funFact: These tiny snails are actually air-breathers with lungs, not gills - they're basically the salt marsh equivalent of land snails that have adapted to live in one of the saltiest terrestrial environments on Earth, handling salt concentrations that would kill most other land creatures!
confusionNotes: Mouse-eared snails might be confused with other tiny salt marsh snails, but their distinctively small size and oval, ear-like shell shape sets them apart - remember 'mouse ear' and look for that characteristic rounded oval that really does look like a miniature mammal ear.
contextualKnowledge: This is a European species that has established itself in New England salt marshes, representing one of many marine and coastal organisms that have crossed the Atlantic. The extremely low observation count in New England (only 5 recorded) suggests they're either very rare, very hard to spot due to their tiny size, or possibly overlooked by most naturalists.
compareHints: As the only Myosotella species recorded in New England, mouse-eared snails are best compared to other members of the Ellobiidae family found in similar salt marsh habitats. They can be distinguished from related hollow-shelled snails by their particularly small size and distinctive oval, mouse ear-shaped shell profile. Other salt marsh snails in the region tend to be either larger or have more elongated or conical shell shapes.
